title: Rama grows up
hook: the four brothers; the bow no one can lift

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king with no sons, and four boys born after the long wait. Your line was some things arrive late. Today, the boys grow up, and one of them is asked to leave home. Day thirty-seven.

Four brothers growing up in a palace. Rama and Lakshmana are inseparable; Bharata and Shatrughna are too. They learn the scriptures, archery, riding, how to rule. Then one day a famous sage walks into the court. Vishvamitra. Demons keep ruining his sacrifices in the forest, and he wants help. Not the army. Not the king. He wants Rama. Who is, the text says, not yet sixteen. Dasharatha, who waited half his life for this boy, panics. Take my army, take me, he says, just not my son. And the family priest, Vasishtha, gently tells the king: let him go. He'll be safe with this teacher. And he'll need what he learns.
screen: `FOUR BROTHERS.` → `THE SAGE WANTS RAMA.` → `NOT YET SIXTEEN.` → `LET HIM GO.`

segments.voice: So Rama and Lakshmana walk out into the forest behind the sage. It's their first time away from home. Vishvamitra teaches them divine weapons and mantras as they walk. They guard his sacrifice, and drive the demons off. One of those demons, Maricha, is knocked far across the sea by a single arrow of Rama's and survives. Hold on to his name; he'll be back. Then the sage says: come with me to Mithila. King Janaka has something you should see. In Janaka's court sits a bow that once belonged to Shiva himself. It's so heavy that, in Valmiki's telling, it's wheeled in on an enormous iron cart dragged by thousands of men. Kings and princes and warriors have come from everywhere to try to lift it. Not one of them could so much as bend it. Janaka has made a promise: whoever can string this bow may marry his daughter, Sita. Rama walks up to the bow. The whole court watches. And he lifts it, as if it were nothing. Here's what the story knows. The bow has been sitting there for years, too heavy for everyone. It was waiting for the one person whose weight it was. Not the strongest man in the room in general. The right person, for this particular weight. Most of us have a bow like that. Something in your family, your work, your street, that everyone else walks past, and that somehow fits your hands. That's your weight. Tomorrow: what happens when Rama tries to string it.
screen: `INTO THE FOREST WITH A TEACHER.` · `MARICHA, KNOCKED ACROSS THE SEA.` · `SHIVA'S BOW, TOO HEAVY FOR ALL.` · `RAMA LIFTS IT.` · then, large: `YOUR WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a thing only you can lift. Sit and breathe. Ask yourself what weight in your life seems shaped for your hands. Something others can't quite carry, or haven't noticed. A relative only you can talk to. A skill. A problem at work nobody else understands. Don't pick it up yet. Just notice it's there, and notice how it feels to think: this one might be mine. The bell holds the time.
Rama grows up. He leaves home with the sage Vishvamitra, learns to fight, and lifts Shiva's bow in Janaka's court when no one else could.
Your line: your weight. Today, lift one thing that everyone else keeps walking past, and see if it fits your hands. Day thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Rama's youth, his journey with Vishvamitra and the lifting of Shiva's bow are favorite scenes in Ramlila plays and in children's retellings of the Ramayana.

fork.setup: you're Dasharatha. a sage asks for your teenage son to fight demons in the forest. what do you do?
options: offer your army and yourself instead.
fork.reveal: he offers everything but Rama. the priest Vasishtha persuades him to let Rama go, and the journey makes him.

original.note: Sanskrit: bow; the bow of Shiva in Janaka's court.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hero is the strongest guy.
what it means: a bow too heavy for everyone waits for the one person whose weight it is.
what a scholar hears: in Valmiki the bow is Shiva's, kept by Janaka; Rama is said to be not yet sixteen when Vishvamitra takes him.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 18–31 (Vishvamitra's request; the forest; Maricha and Subahu)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 66–67 (Janaka's bow in Mithila)

notes: 'Not yet sixteen' follows Dasharatha's words in Bala Kanda 20; confirm.
The bow's cart: Valmiki describes an eight-wheeled iron cart drawn by some thousands (often read as five thousand) men. Script says 'thousands'. Confirm.
The script splits lifting (today) and stringing/breaking (tomorrow); in Valmiki it's one continuous scene. Confirm acceptable.
